missing_areas: physical_optics (beyond a single fringe-spacing proportionality plug-in)
light_photons (calibration-style spectral/series reasoning rather than threshold-only)
issues: Difficulty distribution is not faithful to the source proportions. Projecting the real counts (35:20:8 for levels 1:2:3) to a 9-item test gives approximate targets of 5–6 level-1, 3–4 level-2, and 1–2 level-3 questions. The generated set has {"1":3,"2":3,"3":3}, which is short by at least two level-1 items and has at least one extra level-3 item relative to the allowed ±1 deviation per level.

Coverage is too narrow relative to the calibration set. The generated test omits entire topical areas that appear in the real 2025 examples: no reflection/mirrors items, no refraction/critical-angle/TIR items, no numeric Snell’s-law style computation, no mirror/lens equation numeric image-distance/magnification problem, and no Rydberg/Balmer-style spectral line calculation. Human-eye content is limited to a single conceptual rods-vs-cones question and does not include any diopter/near-point style quantitative vision modeling present in the calibration.

Repetition of reasoning paths: items optics-b-generated-003 and optics-b-generated-007 both focus on Keplerian refracting telescopes with the same core relationships (M = f_obj / f_eye and L = f_obj + f_eye). 003 asks which eyepiece focal length gives larger magnification; 007 asks what happens when changing eyepiece focal length and tube length. These are near-duplicates in conceptual load and both sit in the same optical_instruments niche, reducing breadth.

Several stems are verbose and over-contextualized compared to the concise calibration style. Examples: 006, 007, and 008 include long narrative setups and repeated restatement of formulas and unit hints. The real items are generally tighter, with minimal prose and without didactic reminders like "Shorter wavelength → higher photon energy" or explicit unit conversions in the stem.

Multiple items lean toward generic textbook filler rather than competition-style calibration: 001 (parallel rays through a convex lens) and 002 (role of rods) are very standard conceptual questions with little event-specific nuance. While some such items are acceptable at level 1, the set overuses this style without balancing with more event-specific quantitative or multi-step reasoning.

Difficulty tagging is inconsistent with the calibration. For example: 003 is labeled difficulty 2 but is essentially a direct proportionality recall (M ∝ 1/f_eye) with no calculation, closer to level 1. 004 (image at 2f is same size, real, inverted) is also a standard textbook fact and fits level 1 more than level 2. 005 (magenta solution absorbs green) is a straightforward color-absorption concept and is easier than many level-2 calibration items that require Snell’s law or multi-part classification. Conversely, 006 and 008, while not extremely hard, are more computational than some labeled level-3 calibration items and might be borderline 2–3; the internal scale is not clearly aligned with the source.

Physical optics and light_photons coverage is shallow. 006 is a single proportionality use of Δy = λL/d with no explicit calculation required (just compare fringe spacings), and 008 is a threshold-energy check with heavy scaffolding (formula given, qualitative wavelength–energy relation spelled out, and only four close red wavelengths). The calibration examples for level 3 include more demanding tasks like Brewster-angle computation and Rydberg/Balmer wavelength calculation; the generated items do not reach that style of multi-step reasoning.

Distractors are often too transparent or qualitatively weak. Examples: in 003, option D directly contradicts the formula given in the stem; in 004, the only answer that matches the well-known 2f case is A, and the others mix virtual/inverted in ways that are easy to eliminate; in 005, once magenta is described as missing green, 520 nm is the only plausible choice. This reduces discrimination, especially at the higher labeled difficulties.

Competition faithfulness is weakened by the lack of numeric, equation-based problems that mirror the calibration: no Snell’s-law numeric refraction angle, no diopter/near-point calculation, no mirror equation computation, no Rydberg-series wavelength, and no multi-part classification short-answer. The generated set is entirely multiple choice and skews conceptual, whereas the calibration mix includes numeric and short-answer formats and more quantitative rigor.

Overall, the set is too small in scope, too conceptually repetitive in telescope/optical-instrument content, under-represents key Optics B topics (reflection, refraction/TIR, quantitative imaging, spectral lines), and misaligns difficulty labels and proportions relative to the real 2025 calibration.
